summary: Three paradigms: unstructured (GOTO), procedural (functions + shared global data) and object-oriented (objects that hold their own data and send messages to each other).
Java pipeline: `.java` goes through **javac** (compile time) to bytecode `.class`, then the **JIT compiler inside the JVM** turns it into machine code at run time.
An object has **identity, state and behaviour**. A class is the template, and an object is an instance of it.
OO model = 4 basic components (**Objects, Messages, Methods, Classes**) + 4 main concepts (**Abstraction, Encapsulation/Information Hiding, Inheritance, Polymorphism**).
Polymorphism: the same message is sent to different objects, and each one responds in the way that suits its own class (the slides call it the most powerful OO concept).
mustMemorise: UP: Assembly, COBOL, Basic | PP: C, Pascal, ADA, Fortran | OOP: Java, C++, C#, Objective C, Smalltalk.
The 3 structured constructs: Sequence, Selection, Iteration.
Dates: Smalltalk 1971, C 1972, C++ 1984, Java 1995, C# 2000. People: C = Kernighan & Ritchie (for UNIX), C++ = Stroustrup (AT&T), Java = Gosling (Sun), C# = Hejlsberg (Microsoft).
javac = compile time (source to bytecode). JIT = run time, inside the JVM (bytecode to machine code). JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM.
4 basic components: Objects, Messages, Methods, Classes.
4 main concepts: Abstraction, Encapsulation/Information Hiding, Inheritance, Polymorphism.

Abstraction (Booch): the **essential characteristics** that **distinguish** an object from all other kinds of objects, giving **crisply defined conceptual boundaries**, **relative to the perspective of the viewer**.
Encapsulation = a barrier that protects **private data**, accessed only through **public methods** (get/set). Information hiding = hides the **implementation details** from users.
Methods represent the object's Services, Operations and Interfaces.
Multiple-inheritance clash fixes (per slides): user-specified precedence (Smalltalk), rename one, accept both if signatures differ.

items.title: Three programming paradigms
notes: Unstructured: Assembly, **COBOL**, Basic (GOTO jumps). Procedural: C, Pascal, ADA, Fortran. OOP: Java, C++, C#, Objective C, Smalltalk.
Structured programming uses only **Sequence, Selection, Iteration** (the flowchart on the slide).
Trap: COBOL and Basic are listed as *unstructured*, not procedural.

items.title: Language timeline
notes: Smalltalk 1971, C 1972, C++ 1984, Java 1995, C# 2000 (the red dates).
Simula is the early ancestor of the OO languages (it leads into Smalltalk). C# draws on both C++ and Java.

items.title: Procedural = imperative
notes: Procedural is also called **imperative**. It is built on procedure/function calls.
It is a step-by-step sequence of statements (commands) that uses **assignment** to change variables in memory.

items.title: C language (name typo)
notes: The slide spells it 'Kernihan'. The real name is **Kernighan** (Brian Kernighan & Dennis Ritchie). The two photo captions also appear to be swapped.
Exam facts: C was made to implement **UNIX**, gives access to low-level data, generates efficient code, and its compact code costs readability.

items.title: What OOP is
notes: An object = memory locations + all the operations that can change them.
Computation = objects interacting by **sending messages**. Each object has a **local state** that it can modify.
OO languages: Simula, Smalltalk, C++, Java, C#.

items.title: C++
notes: By **Bjarne Stroustrup (AT&T)**. A superset of C with OO features. Strict type-checking.
The class gives data abstraction and encapsulation.

items.title: C++ is NOT pure OOP
notes: C++ does not force you to use OOP, so you can write non-OO code. Contrast C# on slide 17, which the slides call 'Strictly OO'.

items.title: Java features and slogan
notes: By Sun (James Gosling), originally for embedded consumer goods. Compared with C/C++ it has **no pointers** and **no multiple inheritance**, and its speed issue (interpreted bytecode) is solved by **JIT compilers**.
The slide says 'Compile Once, Run Anywhere'. Sun's real slogan is **'Write Once, Run Anywhere'** (WORA). If an option quotes the slide, accept it.
Trap: 'no multiple inheritance' means of **classes**. A Java class can still implement many interfaces.

items.title: Java translation and execution (JIT vs javac)
notes: Read it top-down: `.java` source, then the **Java Compiler (javac)** at *compile time*, then **bytecode `.class`** (platform-independent), then the **JIT compiler** at *run time*, then native machine code.
The JIT sits **inside the JVM**, and the JVM is part of the **JRE**. The JIT is NOT javac, and it does not produce `.class` files.
JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM. The JDK (not shown on the slide) adds development tools such as `javac` on top of the JRE.

items.title: C#
notes: By Microsoft, led by **Anders Hejlsberg** (creator of Turbo Pascal and Delphi). Based on C++ with Java-like features.
Its features: no pointers, no multiple inheritance, no globals, strictly OO, automatic garbage collection, multi-threading, cross-platform.

items.title: C vs Java program structure
notes: C: global variables + functions calling each other from `main`. Java: data and methods live inside classes (one per file), and a `Driver` class has `main`, which creates objects and calls `a.methodA()`.
The slide title 'C#' is a leftover. The content compares **C vs Java**. `new ClassA(1, 2)` assumes a 2-argument constructor that is not shown.

items.title: Procedural vs OO structure
notes: Left (procedural): Functions 1-4 all read and write one shared **Global Data** blob.
Right (OO): each object bundles its **own Data + Methods**, and objects interact through messages (the arrows). This is encapsulation.
The title 'C#' is wrong again. It means procedural vs OO.

items.title: C vs Java factorial
notes: Same algorithm. Java needs a class, `public static void main(String args[])`, `Scanner` for input and `System.out.println`.

The slide says the file 'must save as Factorial.java'. That is only required for a **public** class. `class Factorial` here is not public, so any file name compiles (checked with JDK 17). Exam rule: a public top-level class must be in `ClassName.java`.
Typo: `" is = “ + getFact(n)` uses a curly quote, which is a compile error in real Java.

items.title: Object characteristics
notes: Exactly three: **Identity, State, Behaviour**.

items.title: Class vs object (Person / Obama)
notes: Identity = Barack Obama. Attributes/state = height, weight, gender, age... Behaviours = eat, study, sleep.
**Person is a Class**. **Obama is an Object (instance) of Person.**

items.title: Car example
notes: Identity = machine serial number. State/properties = colour, max speed. Behaviour/methods = turn, brake, accelerate.

items.title: Four basic components
notes: **Objects**: an entity with attributes (state) + actions.
**Messages**: requests from one object to another to produce a desired result.
**Methods**: descriptions of the operations an object performs when it *receives a message*.
**Classes**: the template for objects (methods + state descriptions). The dumpling mould picture = class, the dumplings = objects.

items.title: Four main concepts (not the same as components)
notes: Concepts: **Abstraction, Encapsulation/Information Hiding, Inheritance, Polymorphism**.
Do not mix them up with the 4 *components* (Objects, Messages, Methods, Classes). 'Message' is a component, not a concept.
The slides pair Encapsulation and Information Hiding as ONE concept.

items.title: Abstraction: Booch definition
notes: Keywords: **essential characteristics**, **distinguish it from all other kinds of objects**, **crisply defined conceptual boundaries**, **relative to the perspective of the viewer**.
Abstraction is about WHAT matters (focus on the essentials). It is not about hiding or protecting data. That is encapsulation/information hiding.

items.title: State and attributes
notes: State (Booch) = all the (usually **static**) properties + the current (usually **dynamic**) **values** of those properties.
Attributes = the data/variables that characterise the state.
Here 'static' means the property *list* does not change. It has nothing to do with the Java keyword `static`.

items.title: Behaviour and the abstraction barrier
notes: Methods represent the **Services** the object provides, the **Operations** it performs on other objects, and the **Interfaces** it provides.
Diagram: the client talks to the object only through its behaviour (the double arrow). The dark ring around the object is the **abstraction barrier**, and the state (Black, 2 doors) stays inside.

items.title: Encapsulation vs information hiding
notes: **Encapsulation** = builds a barrier to protect the object's **private data**. Access goes through **public methods** (get/set).
**Information hiding** = hides the **details/implementation** of the class from users.
Users only need to know **what** a class does and **how to call** its methods. They do **not** need the implementation.
Compare abstraction (slide 28), which is about choosing the essential characteristics relative to the viewer.

items.title: Messages and private internals
notes: Internal state is changed only by the object's own methods, which run in response to **messages**.
The client can send `getACoke()` (public). `getRecipe()` is internal, so a client call to it is marked '???' because it is hidden.

items.title: Why encapsulation / hiding
notes: They help to **protect what you have** and **protect your data**.

items.title: Inheritance terms
notes: Superclass = base class = parent. Subclass = derived class = child.
A subclass may redefine inherited behaviour, which *supersedes* it (overriding). The benefit is reuse without duplicating code.
Trap: 'inherits from one or more classes' is the general OO definition. Java classes can extend only ONE class.

items.title: Inheritance example (Employee)
notes: The **hollow triangle** points to the superclass and means an 'is a/an' relation (generalisation).
SalariedEmployee **adds** an attribute and method (`weeklySalary`, `overtimePay()`). HourlyEmployee **overrides** `earnings()`.
Both inherit firstName, lastName, socialSecurityNo and earnings().

items.title: Multiple inheritance problem
notes: Problem: which property or method to inherit when the same one exists in more than one superclass.
Fixes on the slide: **user-specified precedence (Smalltalk)**, **rename** one, **accept both if signatures differ** (e.g. `print(String s)` / `print(Char c)`, which is overloading).
`Char` is not a Java type (Java has `char`). The slide is language-neutral pseudo-code.

items.title: StudentEmployee diamond-style clash
notes: StudentEmployee has two hollow-triangle arrows, to Student and to Employee.
name, address and age exist in BOTH parents, so it is ambiguous which one to inherit. In Java this cannot be written with classes.

items.title: Polymorphism
notes: Greek for **many shapes / multiple forms**.
The **same message** is sent to **different objects**, and each does the operation appropriate to its class ('do similar things differently').
The sender does not need to know the receiver's class. The slides call it the **most powerful concept of OO**.

items.title: Polymorphism: Animal.move()
notes: `void call(Animal animal) { animal.move(); }` runs Eagle's, Tiger's or Shark's own `move()`, depending on the actual object passed in.
Each subclass overrides `move()`. Which version runs is decided at run time (dynamic binding, covered in Ch5).

items.title: Chapter summary
notes: Re-states 4 components (Objects, Messages, Methods, Classes) + 4 concepts (Abstraction, Encapsulation/Info Hiding, Inheritance, Polymorphism).
The phone diagram uses plain arrows from 2GPhone/3GPhone to MobilePhone, not UML hollow triangles. Treat it as an informal picture.

items.title: OO terms list
notes: Know all of these: object, class, attribute, operation, interface, implementation, association, aggregation, composition, generalisation, super/sub-class, abstract vs concrete class, polymorphism. Ch6 covers the UML for each.
